misconception_description: Student believes that multiple mutually exclusive conditions in a control flow construct must each be written as separate if statements.

solutions.generated_code:
program DamagePokemon
kamus
  attackerTipe, defenderTipe : string
  attackerLevel, defenderLevel : integer
  efektivitas : real
  selisihLevel, damage : integer
algoritma
  input(attackerTipe, attackerLevel)
  input(defenderTipe, defenderLevel)
  efektivitas <- 0.5
  if attackerTipe == defenderTipe then
    efektivitas <- 1
  endif
  if attackerTipe == "fire" and defenderTipe == "grass" then
    efektivitas <- 2
  endif
  if attackerTipe == "grass" and defenderTipe == "water" then
    efektivitas <- 2
  endif
  if attackerTipe == "water" and defenderTipe == "fire" then
    efektivitas <- 2
  endif
  selisihLevel <- attackerLevel - defenderLevel
  damage <- bulat(((2 * attackerLevel) / 5 + 2) * (attackerLevel / defenderLevel) * efektivitas * selisihLevel / 10)
  if damage < 1 then
    damage <- 1
  endif
  output(damage)
endprogram

metadata.modification_notes: The student has replaced the if-elif-else chain with separate if statements, believing this is the correct way to handle mutually exclusive conditions. They set a default effectiveness of 0.5 first, then check each specific condition with separate if statements. Since the type matchup conditions are actually mutually exclusive in this problem (a Pokemon can't simultaneously be fire vs grass AND grass vs water), the code happens to work correctly despite not following best practices. Each condition can only be true once, so there's no issue with later conditions overwriting earlier assignments. However, this approach is less efficient (all conditions are always checked) and less clear in intent than using elif.
